name: Category Theory
description: A lens for composing Factors from the language of mathematical structure, universal properties, and relationships-between-relationships. Maps categorical concepts—categories, functors, natural transformations, limits, adjunctions, monads, and topoi—to the 19-node topology. Useful for Factors involving compositionality, structure-preserving maps, adjoint relationships, and the deep unity of mathematical constructions.

x.note: The depth anchor—(f∘g)∘h = f∘(g∘h). In the invariant core, x initiates the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, linking associativity to presheaves, universal arrows, and identities.

y.note: The relational anchor—id_B ∘ f = f = f ∘ id_A. Completes the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, showing how identities close the Yoneda loop.

z.note: The transformational anchor—Hom(𝒞(−, A), F) ≅ F(A). Connected persistently to 0 (category/terminal object), reflecting the terminal object’s role in Yoneda embedding.

0.note: The whole category observed as a unified system of objects and arrows. Persistently connected to z (Yoneda lemma).

1.note: A boundary within the category. Forms a 4‑cycle 1→6→5→2→1 with natural transformations, functors, and objects, capturing the subcategory‑object‑functor‑natural transformation loop.

2.note: Primitives—the objects of the category. Part of the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle; the building block that closes back to subcategory via the cycle.

3.note: The invariant law—associative composition of morphisms. A node in the 7‑core; connected to adjunction (c) and endofunctor (e).

4.note: The fundamental relation—arrows between objects. A node in the 7‑core; connects to Grothendieck topology (b) and topos (f).

5.note: The pattern that maps between categories. Part of the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle; bridges objects and natural transformations.

6.note: The transformation between functors. Part of the 1‑6‑5‑2 cycle; the morphism of functors.

7.note: The realization of universal property—the cone that is terminal among all cones. Persistently connected to 8 (colimit), reflecting the limit‑colimit duality.

8.note: The granularity—the cocone that is initial among all cocones. Persistently connected to 7 (limit), capturing the dual nature of universal constructions.

9.note: The event—the unique arrow that factors through a universal construction. Part of the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, placing it between presheaves and identities.

a.note: Pure potential—all possible contravariant functors to Set. Initiates the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x, linking to associativity, universal arrows, and identities.

b.note: The arena of coverage—the sieves that determine when a presheaf is a sheaf. A node in the 7‑core; connected to morphism (4), monad (d), and topos (f).

c.note: Directional bias—a pair of functors with natural bijection. A node in the 7‑core; connected to composition (3) and morphism (4).

d.note: Persistent structure—an endofunctor with unit and multiplication. A node in the 7‑core; connected to Grothendieck topology (b) and topos (f).

e.note: The active algorithm—a functor from a category to itself. A node in the 7‑core; connected to composition (3) and Grothendieck topology (b).

f.note: The resonant cavity—a category that behaves like the category of sets. A node in the 7‑core; connected to morphism (4), monad (d), adjunction (c), and composition (3).

n.interpretation: Categorical dimension / Complexity of diagram shape

values.n=1: Poset / Preorder — at most one morphism between objects
values.n=2: Monoid / Group — one object, many morphisms
values.n=3: Small category — objects and morphisms form sets
values.n=4: Locally small category — Hom-sets are sets
values.n=5: Large category — proper class of objects

n.formula: n corresponds to the 'size' and 'dimension' of the categorical structure

m.formula: m = log₂(complexity of enrichment monoidal structure)

phase.special: For limits: phase = 0 when terminal cone exists; for colimits: phase = π when initial cocone exists
phase.significance: Phase measures how 'universal' a construction is—how close to satisfying the universal property

object_view.description: The Factor viewed as a category of objects and morphisms
object_view.phase_condition: Phase as existence of universal properties—0 for limits, π for colimits

functor_view.description: The Factor viewed as a functor between categories
functor_view.phase_condition: Phase as fullness/faithfulness—0 for fully faithful, π/2 for essentially surjective

adjunction_view.description: The Factor viewed as an adjoint pair (F ⊣ G)
adjunction_view.phase_condition: Phase as unit-counit composition—0 when η_G = id, π when ε_F = id

topos_view.description: The Factor viewed as a topos (generalized universe of sets)
topos_view.phase_condition: Phase as truth value in subobject classifier—Ω has 2^m truth values

creating_anew.note: When creating a categorical structure, start with objects (node 2) and morphisms (node 4), let composition (node 3) provide the invariant laws, and seek universal properties (nodes 7‑9).

translating_known.set_category: Map to Set: node 0 as Set, node 2 as sets, node 4 as functions, node 7 as products, node 8 as coproducts
translating_known.functor_category: Map to [𝒞,𝒟]: node 5 as objects (functors), node 6 as morphisms (natural transformations)
translating_known.adjunction: Map to F ⊣ G: node c as the adjunction, node 9 as the unit and counit universal arrows
translating_known.monad: Map to (T,η,μ): node d as monad, node e as endofunctor T, node 6 as natural transformations η, μ
translating_known.topos: Map to 𝒯: node f as topos, node a as presheaves, node b as Grothendieck topology

temporary_note.special: A category defined only by its objects, with morphisms not yet specified. Awaiting the grammar of connection.

constraints.associativity: Node x ensures composition is associative—(f∘g)∘h = f∘(g∘h).
constraints.identities: Node y ensures identity morphisms exist—id_B ∘ f = f = f ∘ id_A.
constraints.yoneda_embedding: Node z ensures the Yoneda lemma holds—Hom(𝒞(−, A), F) ≅ F(A).
constraints.functor_preservation: Node 5 (functors) must preserve composition and identities.
constraints.naturality: Node 6 (natural transformations) must satisfy naturality squares.
constraints.stratum_preference: global for foundational categorical work; trefoil_c for universal properties; trefoil_g for natural transformations; fig8 for higher categories and topoi.
constraints.invariant_core: The Category Theory paradigm respects the persistent skeleton from trefoil_i, which decomposes into five subsystems that mirror the invariant structure of the T(19,2) knot. These subsystems provide a pedagogical roadmap: (1) the simple edge 0→z linking the category to the Yoneda lemma, (2) the edge 8→7 linking colimit to limit, (3) the 4‑cycle x→a→9→y→x capturing the Yoneda‑universal property loop, (4) the 4‑cycle 1→6→5→2→1 capturing the subcategory‑functor‑natural transformation cycle, and (5) the 7‑node core {3,4,b,c,d,e,f} encoding the algebraic heart of category theory (composition, morphisms, Grothendieck topologies, adjunctions, monads, endofunctors, topoi).
